sentences.text: After purchasing the aforesaid plot, the plaintiff constructed a house on the said plot.

In the year 2004, DDA officials carried out demolition in the area and a big part of the house of the plaintiff was demolished and approximately half portion of the said plot was acquired by DDA for a park.

Out of the total 150 sq yds, the plaintiff remained owner of 75 sq yds only.

As the house was inhabitable, the plaintiff collected all the material on her plot and built three temporary/kaccha rooms/jhuggies in the area measuring about 25 sq yds which were covered with polythene sheds and the rest portion of the plot remained vacant.

4. It is further averred that in the month of November, 2009, the defendant tried to construct one another jhuggi on the remaining vacant portion on which the plaintiff objected.
The plaintiff realized that the defendant is trying to grab the property and hence she asked the defendant to vacate the suit property.
The plaintiff also required the premises as the marriage of son of the plaintiff was to be solemnized.
However, defendant prolonged the matter on one pretext or the other and did not vacate the suit property.

In the month of January, 2010, the plaintiff pressed hard and asked the defendant to vacate the suit property, but instead of vacating the suit property, the defendant filed a false and frivolous suit for permanent injunction against the son of plaintiff which was dismissed as compromised.

Thereafter again plaintiff requested the defendant to vacate the suit property to which defendant flatly refused and even tried to take forcible possession of the vacant land in front of the suit property and threatened to create third party interest in the suit property by further using gunda elements on 28.04.2013.
Hence, the present suit.

The normal rule which governs civil proceedings is that a fact can be said to be established if it is proved by a preponderance of probabilities.
The belief regarding the existence of a fact thus be founded on a balance of probabilities.
Preponderance' is used for it carries or conveys the idea that the conscience of the judge is important in appreciation of evidence and law in civil matters.
In the process of appreciation of evidence, the 'slight' evidence may 'tilt the balance' in Civil cases on applying the principle of 'preponderance'.
Therefore, it is said that the evidence is to be weighed.

In Narayan Ganesh Dastane v. Sucheta Narayan Dastane, AIR 1975 SC 1534, our Hon'ble Apex Court observed as under:
"The normal rule which governs civil proceedings is that a fact can be said to be established if it is proved by a preponderance of probabilities.

entities.text: Narayan Ganesh Dastane v. Sucheta Narayan Dastane, AIR 1975 SC 1534
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
This is for the reason that under the Evidence Act, Sec. 3, a fact is said to be proved when the court either believes it to exist or considers its existence so probable that a prudent man ought,
under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that it exists.

The belief regarding the existence CS No. 58215/16 Smt. Dharam Biro Vs. Smt.
Soniya Devi Page: 11 of 13 -:: 12 ::-
of a fact may thus be founded on a balance of probabilities.

entities.text:
CS No. 58215/16 Smt. Dharam Biro Vs. Smt.
Soniya Devi
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A prudent man faced with conflicting probabilities concerning a fact-situation will act on the supposition that the fact exists, if on weighing the various probabilities he finds that the preponderance is in favour of the existence of the particular fact.

As a prudent man,
so the court applies this test for finding whether a fact in issue can be said to be proved.
The first step in this process is to fix the probabilities, the second to weigh them, though the two may often intermingle.
The impossible is weeded out at the first stage, the improbable at the second.

Within the wide range of probabilities the court has often a difficult choice to make but it is this choice which ultimately determines where the preponderance of probabilities lies."
23.

From the evidence on record and especially the cross examination of PW1/plaintiff and PW3/Nusrat Ali shows that on weighing the evidence and the documents filed on record and on the basis of principle of preponderance of probabilities, the cross examination of PW1/plaintiff and PW3/Nusrat Ali as well as document Ex. PW1/16 even weaken the case of the plaintiff.

Furthermore,
the plaintiff has also miserably failed to prove that DDA had acquired half of the land out of the total land having been purchased by him.
24. In view of above, all these issues are decided against the plaintiff.
